subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 6 periods = 240 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

periods.textbook_anchor: Plants and Animals Live Together — Students discuss which animals from the picture spread they have seen before, describing size using hands and arms (p. 64)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 63 picture spread of twelve animals near plant parts

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Think of a tree or bush you walk past every day — what living things have you noticed on it or near it?' Students share briefly in pairs, then a few pairs report to the class. The teacher writes animal names on the board as they emerge.

Students open Textbook p. 63 and scan the picture spread of twelve animals. The teacher names each animal aloud and invites students to use their fingers, hands, and arms to show how big or small each one is — 'Show me how big an elephant is! Now show me how small an ant is!' Students identify which of these animals they have personally seen and describe where.

The teacher reads aloud the 'Do you know?' panel on Textbook p. 64. For each animal–plant relationship mentioned (camel eating leaves, owl nesting in hollows, squirrels using twigs, sunbirds drinking nectar, tailorbird stitching leaves), the teacher pauses and asks: 'Why do you think this animal stays close to plants?' Students respond orally, building toward the central idea that plants provide food, shelter, and places to raise young.

The class gathers responses around three headings the teacher has written on the board: Food / Shelter / Raising young. Students call out which heading fits each animal discussed. The teacher closes by posing the question from Textbook p. 64 as an open wondering: 'Why do these animals choose to live near plants?' — leaving it as a question students carry with them.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain, using examples from their surroundings, how animals depend on plants for food, shelter, and raising young.
periods.section_context: Twelve animals (frog, tailorbird, elephants, squirrels, ants, caterpillar, butterfly, woodpecker, moth, barbet, stink bug, earthworms) shown near plant parts; Do you know? panel: camel, owl, squirrel, crow, monkey, sunbird, butterfly, tailorbird, bat, leopard, caterpillar and their plant relationships.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether their families have noticed particular animals returning to the same tree or plant each season — this draws out intergenerational observation naturally. Organise sharing in pairs first so quieter students have a low-stakes entry before whole-class discussion.

periods.textbook_anchor: Life in the Soil — Students pick up soil near a plant, observe its look, feel, smell, and check for leaves or insects (p. 64)
materials: Access to a patch of soil near a plant on the school grounds (or soil samples collected in small containers before the unit)
Student notebook or loose paper for recording

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses a quick question: 'What do you think soil is made of?' Students call out ideas freely. The teacher does not correct — this is a before-inquiry probe.

Students go to the school garden or work with containers of soil brought in from near a plant. Following the task on Textbook p. 64, each student picks up a small pinch of soil and observes: its colour, whether it is dry or damp, rough or smooth, hard or grainy. They check whether leaves, roots, or insects are present. Finally, they smell the soil and try to describe the smell in words. The teacher circulates, prompting: 'What does it feel like between your fingers? Is it all the same, or do you feel different things mixed in?'

Students record their observations in their notebooks with a simple format: Colour / Feel / Dry or damp? / Smell / What else did I find? The teacher ensures every student completes at least one written observation before the class reconvenes.

The class shares findings. The teacher asks: 'Did everyone's soil look and feel exactly the same? Why might soil near a plant feel different from soil in an open dry patch?' The teacher introduces the idea that soil near plants contains old leaves, roots, and tiny creatures — setting up the content the textbook describes about soil as a living system. Students revisit the content_summary question: what is soil made of?

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple sensory investigation of a natural material and record their observations in words.
periods.section_context: Soil near a plant: colour, texture (rough, smooth, hard, grainy), moisture (dry or damp), smell, presence of leaves, roots, insects; soil as a mix of broken rock fragments, old leaves, roots, stems, and living and dead animals.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage students to describe the smell of soil in their own words — some communities associate the smell of wet earth with seasonal change or farming; welcome these descriptions. Pair students so that those hesitant to touch soil have a partner to observe alongside before trying themselves.

periods.activity_title: Spotting Animals Near Our Plant Friend
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in the Soil — Students stand near their plant friend, spot animals, describe them in words, and fill in the observation table (p. 66)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 66 animal pictures provided as visual reference for identification

time_bands.activity: The teacher leads a brief preparatory discussion: 'When you go to stand near a plant, what should you do first — move quickly and talk loudly, or stand still and wait quietly?' Students share; the teacher establishes that animals show themselves more readily when observers are calm and quiet.

Students move to the school garden (or observe a potted plant near a window). Each student stands near a plant, stays as still as possible, and looks carefully for any animals — on leaves, in the soil, on branches, in the air nearby. They refer to Textbook p. 66 pictures if they need help identifying what they see. For each animal spotted, students note its name (or describe it), where exactly it was (on a leaf, in the soil, on a stem), and what it seemed to be doing.

Back in class, students fill the observation table in Textbook p. 66, describing each animal in words. The teacher asks a few students to share one animal they spotted and where they found it, building a class list on the board.

The teacher connects the sightings to the monsoon discussion from the textbook: 'If we did this observation right after heavy rain, do you think we would see more animals or fewer? Where do you think the extra ones come from?' Students respond orally — this sets up the concept of seasonal change in animal presence without resolving it in a way that requires a future unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the presence and location of animals in a natural setting using a structured description.
periods.section_context: Animals spotted near a plant friend: location on plant parts (leaf, stem, branch, soil surface, in soil); insects such as ants, termites, beetles, grasshoppers, earthworms, millipedes; observation table recording animal name, location, and behaviour.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether the kinds of animals they see around plants change with the weather or the time of year — this invites seasonal and local knowledge without requiring the teacher to supply it. Allow students who could not spot a live animal to describe one they have seen near a plant on another occasion.

periods.activity_title: Listening for Birds — Sound and Direction
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in the Soil — Students close their eyes, listen for bird sounds, cup their ears to localise sound, and record bird names and sounds in a table (p. 68)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Have you ever heard a bird call and tried to find it with your eyes? What made it hard or easy to spot?' Students share briefly. The teacher explains that ears can help us find the direction a sound is coming from.

Students step outside (or sit near open windows) and close their eyes for an unhurried listening stretch. Following the task on Textbook p. 68, they listen carefully for bird sounds. When they hear one, they cup both hands behind their ears, turn slowly to face the direction the sound seems loudest, and then open their eyes to look for the bird. Students repeat this for any different bird sounds they hear. The teacher participates alongside students, modelling the ear-cupping and direction-finding behaviour.

Back in class, students open Textbook p. 68 and fill the sound-recording table: the name of the bird (or a description if they do not know the name), the sound it made (written as they would describe it — koo-koo, tweet, tuk-tuk, etc.), and the time of day. The teacher invites students to try producing the sounds they heard, and classmates guess which bird it might be.

The teacher facilitates a short discussion: 'If you heard no bird sounds at all, what might explain that? Do you think you would hear more bird sounds early in the morning, in the afternoon, or in the evening?' Students reason aloud. The class settles on the idea that birds, like other animals, have patterns in their activity — and that quiet listening is itself a skill of observation.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use directed listening and simple ear-cupping technique to localise sounds in the environment and record what they hear.
periods.section_context: Bird sounds heard near a plant; ear-cupping technique for sound localisation; sound-recording table (bird name or description, sound written in words, time of day); variation in bird activity across morning, afternoon, evening.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Invite students to share bird names or calls they know in their home language — many students will recognise local birds by sound before they know the textbook name. Ask whether any student has heard an elder imitate a bird call or use bird sounds to predict weather or season.

periods.activity_title: Drawing Our Plant Friend with Animal Spots
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students draw their plant friend and use coloured dots to mark where they spotted animals, birds, or insects (p. 71)
materials: Coloured crayons or colour pencils (at least three colours)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 70–71 Let us reflect pages as reference for the drawing task

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to close their eyes and picture the plant they observed during their outdoor activity — its shape, its leaves, any branches. Then the teacher says: 'Now try to remember — where exactly did you see an animal, insect, or bird on or near that plant? On a leaf? In the soil underneath? On a branch?' Students share a few vivid memories aloud before beginning to draw.

Students open Textbook p. 71 and follow the drawing task. They draw their plant friend as carefully as they can, showing its overall shape, leaves, stem, and roots if visible. Then they use different coloured dots to mark the places where they spotted animals — the teacher suggests assigning one colour to insects, another to birds, and a third to soil animals, but allows students to choose their own system. Each student labels or writes a word near each dot to name the animal.

Students pair up and explain their drawings to each other: 'I saw an ant here on this leaf, and I saw an earthworm down here in the soil.' The partner asks one question about the drawing. This oral explanation consolidates the observation experience through spoken expression.

The teacher gathers the class briefly: 'Look at how many different places animals were found on just one plant. What does that tell us about the plant?' Students respond with one or two ideas, closing the activity on the central chapter insight that plants are homes and food sources for many animals.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent their field observations through labelled drawing, indicating where different animals were found in relation to a plant.
periods.section_context: Drawing of plant friend; coloured dot system marking locations of spotted animals (insects, birds, soil animals) on and around the plant; labels or written names beside each dot; oral explanation to a partner.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Accept drawings that are simple or schematic — the goal is meaningful placement of the coloured dots, not artistic precision. Ask students whether their drawing shows any animals their partner did not notice, to spark curiosity about the variety of life near plants.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students consult an elder and arrange the stages of a caterpillar's life cycle in correct order (p. 71)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 71 life-cycle sequencing task with the five stages listed

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Has anyone ever seen a caterpillar on a leaf? Has anyone ever seen it turn into something else?' Students share experiences. The teacher then reads aloud the five jumbled stages from Textbook p. 71 one by one — 'Now it was a butterfly. The caterpillar formed a cocoon. It flew away gently. One day it stopped eating. It came out of the cocoon.' — without giving the order, and asks students to listen carefully.

Students work individually to write the five stages in the order they think is correct in their notebooks. The teacher circulates without confirming or correcting — students rely on their own reasoning. The teacher then invites two or three volunteers to share their sequence and explain why they placed the stages in that order.

The teacher leads a whole-class discussion: 'The task says to consult an elder person. Why might an elder know something about this that we might not?' Students discuss. The teacher notes that grandparents, farmers, and gardeners have watched these changes happen across many seasons and that asking them is a way of learning from lived experience. The class then agrees on the correct sequence together and writes it on the board: caterpillar eats → one day it stops eating → it forms a cocoon → it comes out of the cocoon → now it is a butterfly and flies away.

The teacher returns to the chapter's opening question: 'We have seen that animals live on, around, and under plants. We have also seen that animals change through their lives. How does a plant help a caterpillar at each stage?' Students give a few oral responses, connecting plant-as-food and plant-as-shelter to the life cycle stages. The teacher closes by affirming that watching nature closely — the way the activities in this chapter asked them to — is how people have learned about plants and animals for a very long time.

periods.implied_lo: Students can arrange the stages of an animal's life cycle in the correct sequence and explain what happens at each stage.
periods.section_context: Caterpillar life-cycle sequencing: five stages — caterpillar eating, stopping eating, forming a cocoon, emerging from the cocoon, butterfly flying away; role of consulting an elder in understanding natural change; connection between plant and caterpillar at each life stage.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether any student has heard a family member or neighbour tell a story about a caterpillar or butterfly — this surfaces intergenerational and local ecological knowledge naturally. Encourage students to think about where the caterpillar was living (on a plant) at each stage, connecting the life cycle to the chapter's core idea.

assessment_items.question_text: A tailorbird was seen stitching leaves together near a tree. Why does the tailorbird stay close to this plant?

options.label: A
options.text: To drink water that collects on the leaves.

options.label: B
options.text: To eat the insects that live inside the tree trunk.

options.label: C
options.text: To hide from the sun under the leaves.

options.label: D
options.text: To use the leaves to build a nest for its young ones.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. The tailorbird's leaf-stitching nest is explicitly described in the Do you know? panel. Distractors represent plausible but incorrect uses of plants.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain, using examples from their surroundings, how animals depend on plants for food, shelter, and raising young.

competency.competency_text: Identifies needs of plants, birds, and animals, and how they can be supported (water, soil, food, care)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the tailorbird's plant use with a water-collection function — shows a general association with plants but not the specific nesting relationship described in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Attributes a shade-seeking motive to the tailorbird — a plausible animal behaviour but not what the chapter teaches about this bird's relationship with plants.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the tailorbird (leaf-stitcher) with the woodpecker (tree-trunk resident) — a within-chapter confusion between two birds introduced in the same section.

assessment_items.question_text: A student picked up a small amount of soil from near a plant. She noticed the soil felt damp and rough, had a strong smell, and contained a small piece of leaf and a tiny insect. What does this soil tell us about what it is made of?
expected_elements: Soil contains broken rock or rock fragments (giving the rough, grainy texture).
Soil contains old or decaying plant matter such as leaves and roots (the leaf piece is evidence of this).
Soil contains living or dead animals (the tiny insect is an example of a living animal in soil).
The damp texture and smell show that soil near a plant holds moisture and has organic material decomposing in it.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks for a response that names at least three components (rock/mineral particles, plant matter, living organisms) and links them to what the student in the question observed. Partial credit for two components correctly identified.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple sensory investigation of a natural material and record their observations in words.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Soil contains broken rock fragments — this explains the rough or grainy texture.
Soil contains old leaves, roots, or stems — the leaf piece found is direct evidence.
Soil contains living or dead animals — the tiny insect found is an example.
Soil near a plant is damp and has an organic smell because of the plant matter and moisture present.

assessment_items.question_text: A student stood quietly near a plant and looked carefully for animals. She found an ant on a leaf, an earthworm in the soil, and a beetle on a stem. Which of the following best describes what her observation shows?

options.label: A
options.text: Animals come near plants only when it rains.

options.label: B
options.text: Different animals live in different parts of and around a plant.

options.label: C
options.text: Only insects live near plants; larger animals live far away.

options.label: D
options.text: Plants grow better when no animals are around them.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. The observation table activity in this section is designed to show that plants host animals in diverse locations — leaves, soil, stems, branches. Distractors target common overgeneralisations.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the presence and location of animals in a natural setting using a structured description.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.C: Overgeneralises from the insects observed — the student has not connected the earthworm (soil animal, not an insect) to the broader idea that many kinds of animals live near plants.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates the monsoon discussion (more animals appear after rain) with the idea that animals are only present during rain — a misreading of the seasonal pattern described in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Inverts the plant–animal relationship — may reflect a misconception that animals damage plants rather than that plants and animals live together in a mutually present community.

assessment_items.question_text: A student cupped her hands behind her ears and turned slowly in a circle while listening outdoors. She heard a bird sound that became loudest when she faced a particular direction. How does cupping your ears help you find where a bird sound is coming from? Give one reason.
expected_elements: Cupping the hands behind the ears helps collect more sound, making the sound louder or clearer.
Turning to face the direction where the sound is loudest tells you which direction the bird is in.
The student can then look in that direction to try to spot the bird.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks for a response that correctly links ear-cupping to gathering more sound and explains how direction is found by turning until the sound is loudest. A partial response that mentions only one of these two steps should receive partial credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use directed listening and simple ear-cupping technique to localise sounds in the environment and record what they hear.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

expected_elements: Cupped hands act like a larger ear, gathering more sound so it seems louder or clearer.
Turning slowly while listening allows the student to find the direction from which the sound is loudest.
Facing the loudest direction and then opening the eyes helps the student locate the bird visually.

assessment_items.task: Draw a plant that you have seen — it can be a tree, a bush, or a potted plant. Using three different colours, mark with dots the places where you have seen or think you might find: (1) an insect, (2) a bird, and (3) a soil animal. Write the name or a description of the animal next to each dot.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My plant: ___________
Insect (colour: ___): where — ___________, name or description — ___________
Bird (colour: ___): where — ___________, name or description — ___________
Soil animal (colour: ___): where — ___________, name or description — ___________
format_of_output: Three coloured dots in different locations on the drawing
Written name or description next to each dot
assessment_items.annotation: Assess the drawing on meaningful placement of dots (each in a plausible location — insect on leaf or stem, bird on branch or near plant, soil animal in or near the soil at the base) and the accuracy of the label. Accept any locally known plant and any correctly placed animal. Regional variation in plant and animal names is entirely expected and acceptable — award full marks for any locally accurate example.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent their field observations through labelled drawing, indicating where different animals were found in relation to a plant.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate their outdoor observation of animals near a plant into a visual-spatial representation, showing that different animals occupy different parts of a plant's environment.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold ensures each of the three animal types (insect, bird, soil animal) is separately addressed. Look for whether the student has placed each dot in a location consistent with where that type of animal is actually found — not just placed dots randomly.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: dots are placed in ecologically plausible locations (insect on leaf/stem, bird on branch or nearby, earthworm or ant in soil); labels are specific or descriptive. Weak: dots are placed without ecological logic (bird in soil); labels are absent or too vague to identify the animal type.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who have difficulty drawing may describe the plant in words and write where each animal is found. Students who do not know the name of a bird or insect should describe its appearance or call — this counts fully.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing with labelled coloured dots directly mirrors the Let us reflect task in the textbook and requires students to make a spatial judgement about habitat that a written-only response cannot capture.

assessment_items.question_text:
Read the five mixed-up events below and write them in the correct order to show how a caterpillar becomes a butterfly:
• Now it was a butterfly.
• The caterpillar formed a cocoon.
• It flew away gently.
• One day it stopped eating.
• It came out of the cocoon.
Write the events in the correct order, numbered 1 to 5.
expected_elements: 1. One day it stopped eating.
2. The caterpillar formed a cocoon.
3. It came out of the cocoon.
4. Now it was a butterfly.
5. It flew away gently.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks for all five stages in the correct order. Award partial credit (3 out of 5) if the student correctly sequences steps 1–3 (stopping eating → cocoon → emerging) even if steps 4 and 5 are swapped. The key biological logic is: stop eating → form cocoon → emerge → become butterfly → fly away.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can arrange the stages of an animal's life cycle in the correct sequence and explain what happens at each stage.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Stage 1: One day it stopped eating. (The caterpillar prepares for transformation by ceasing to eat.)
Stage 2: The caterpillar formed a cocoon. (It wraps itself in a protective casing.)
Stage 3: It came out of the cocoon. (After transformation inside, it emerges.)
Stage 4: Now it was a butterfly. (The emerged creature is identified as a butterfly.)
Stage 5: It flew away gently. (The butterfly takes flight, completing the cycle.)
